job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Meridian Ocean Minerals. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Meridian Ocean Minerals is a deep-sea mining company headquartered in Houston, with a policy office in Washington, DC. Our mission is to commercially recover polymetallic nodules from the deep seabed, a vast source of nickel, cobalt, manganese, and copper, and to supply these critical minerals for batteries, the energy transition, and economic growth. We believe the United States must lead in this industry. Our policy team works with lawmakers to protect our ability to continue exploration and commercial development.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which would shut down our core work and which we strongly oppose. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 drafting review (text as amended Oct. 6, 2026)

Each item is tagged **[Loophole]** (lets activity continue), **[Enforcement]** (hard to administer or prove), or **[Challenge]** (legally vulnerable or internally inconsistent).

## Definitions (Sec. 2)

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "by a single vessel" [Loophole].** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per vessel, not per operator, affiliate, or project. A fleet of vessels each under the line, or transshipment between vessels, falls outside the definition, and there is no aggregation or anti-structuring rule.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "per year" and tonnage [Enforcement].** The bill doesn't say whether "year" is a calendar year, rolling 12 months, or license year. It also doesn't say whether tons are wet or dry, in situ or lifted, or with or without sediment. Nodules carry significant moisture, so the threshold could be argued either way.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "recovery" and "depths greater than 200 meters" [Enforcement].** "Recovery" is undefined: it could mean collection on the seafloor, lifting to the surface, or retention on board. The bill also gives no reference point or datum for measuring depth.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A), "other mineral resources" [Challenge].** The language arguably sweeps in deepwater oil and gas and floating production vessels, which routinely exceed both the tonnage and vessel-size thresholds. That overbreadth invites vagueness arguments and may bring in opponents outside our usual coalition.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(B), undefined "Secretary" [Challenge].** The bill never defines "Secretary," while Sec. 6 specifies "Secretary of State." It's unclear whether Commerce, Interior, or another official makes the determination.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(B), standard and procedure [Challenge].** "Risks... comparable to" Subparagraph (A) activities supplies no intelligible principle, criteria, notice, comment, or publication requirement. Because Sec. 5(b) attaches criminal penalties, this invites nondelegation, fair-notice, and void-for-vagueness challenges, and the rule of lenity would apply. The bill also doesn't say whether a determination applies only prospectively.

7. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person" [Loophole].** The definition covers only citizens and "corporation[s] organized under the laws of a State." It omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and joint ventures, entities organized under federal, D.C., or territorial law, and permanent residents. Foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. parents are also outside it, so restructuring through one avoids coverage.

8. **Sec. 2(3) and Sec. 4(a), "covered vessel" [Loophole/Enforcement].** The 5,000 gross ton threshold has no relationship to the 10,000-ton recovery threshold. Smaller vessels, barges, platforms, and unmanned systems escape registration, and "equipped for the recovery" is undefined. The registry would also capture vessels exempt under Sec. 3(b) and 3(c).

## Prohibition and exemptions (Sec. 3)

9. **Sec. 3(a), "person in the United States" [Enforcement].** The phrase is undefined. It's unclear whether it reaches the territorial sea, EEZ, or continental shelf, or persons directing operations remotely. Foreign entities operating abroad with no U.S. person involved are outside the prohibition.

10. **Sec. 3(a), scope of prohibited conduct [Loophole].** The bill bars only "engag[ing] in" mining. It doesn't reach financing, supplying, transporting, processing, importing, or buying nodules, or minority investment in foreign operations. It has no express aiding-and-abetting provision for civil liability.

11. **Sec. 3(a) with Sec. 2(1), sub-threshold activity [Loophole].** Exploration, pilot, and test mining below the threshold remain lawful, with no cap on duration or number of campaigns. Companies can build capability and data under the line.

12. **Sec. 3(b), "exploration license" [Loophole/Challenge].** The term is undefined. It doesn't say who must issue the license (NOAA, a foreign sponsoring state, an ISA-linked contract), so foreign-issued licenses held by U.S. persons may or may not qualify.

13. **Sec. 3(b), "mining conducted under" a license [Enforcement].** Exploration licenses generally don't authorize commercial recovery, so what is exempt is unclear. The text could cover only exploration-scale work or everything done under the license. It also never addresses commercial recovery permits, and "mining" is undefined in Sec. 3(b), unlike "commercial deep seabed mining" in 3(a).

14. **Sec. 3(b), open-ended grandfathering [Loophole].** There is no expiration, volume cap, or area limit, and no compliance condition. The bill is silent on renewal, extension, modification, and transfer or assignment to affiliates.

15. **Sec. 3(b) with Secs. 5(a) and 8, timing cutoffs [Loophole/Challenge].** Protection runs to licenses issued before enactment, but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. That invites a rush of license issuance. Pending applicants and those who invested in reliance on the permitting path have a basis for takings and due process claims, which means litigation risk.

16. **Sec. 3(c), environmental assessment exemption [Loophole].** The test is purpose-based and undefined. There is no volume cap, duration limit, government approval, bar on selling recovered material, or reporting requirement. Large "assessment" campaigns could qualify, and mixed-purpose operations would turn on intent.

17. **Whole bill, no interaction with existing law [Challenge].** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq.) or address OCSLA. It doesn't tell NOAA to stop accepting applications or issuing licenses and permits. A permit issued under DSHMRA could be argued to authorize conduct that Sec. 3 prohibits. Counsel should confirm the statutory details.

## Registry (Sec. 4)

18. **Sec. 4(a), registration [Enforcement].** The bill sets no deadline, standards, rulemaking authority, or fee, and doesn't define "operator." NOAA has no stated power to deny or revoke registration. There is no jurisdictional hook for foreign-flag vessels.

19. **Sec. 4(b), reporting [Enforcement].** "Describing the recovery activities" doesn't require tonnage, location, depth, destination, or sales. Nothing allows the government to verify the 10,000-ton threshold. Reports are self-certified, with no audit or inspection rights, recordkeeping rules, or public disclosure.

20. **Sec. 4 with Sec. 5, no penalty for registry violations [Enforcement].** Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3. Failing to register or file has no specified consequence, and false reports would depend on general statutes such as 18 U.S.C. 1001.

## Enforcement and penalties (Sec. 5)

21. **Sec. 5, no enforcing agency or tools [Enforcement].** The bill doesn't say who investigates, assesses penalties, or sues. It gives no inspection, boarding, subpoena, seizure, or forfeiture authority, and no power to seek injunctions. The Coast Guard and DOJ are not mentioned.

22. **Sec. 5(a), civil penalty process [Challenge].** There is no administrative procedure, notice and hearing, penalty factors, or judicial review provision, and no inflation adjustment. A cap of $1,000,000 per day invites Excessive Fines and due process challenges as applied.

23. **Sec. 5(a) with Sec. 8, retroactivity conflict [Challenge].** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act takes effect 180 days later. It's unclear whether gap-period conduct is penalized. If it is, there are retroactivity and fair-notice problems.

24. **Sec. 5(a) with Sec. 2(1)(A), "each day on which the violation occurs" [Enforcement].** The offense is defined by an annual tonnage threshold, so it's unclear when a violation begins. The bill doesn't say whether days before the threshold is crossed count, or whether each later day is separate. Limitations accrual is also unclear.

25. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully" [Enforcement].** The mental state is undefined. Courts may require proof that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful, including knowledge of threshold crossing, license status, and any Sec. 2(1)(B) determination. The bill has no responsible-corporate-officer language.

## International and duration (Secs. 6–7)

26. **Sec. 6 [Enforcement].** "Shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months" doesn't say whether the deadline applies to starting talks or concluding an agreement. "Equivalent" is undefined, and there is no consequence for missing the deadline and no reporting to Congress. It also doesn't say whether the result would be a treaty needing Senate advice and consent. The provision is hortatory.

27. **Sec. 7(a) vs. 7(b) [Challenge].** The prohibition lasts until Congress acts, yet the Act sunsets after 10 years regardless. The text doesn't say which controls. The "durable" off-ramp in 7(a) is moot if 7(b) governs.

28. **Sec. 7(b), no savings clause [Enforcement].** On sunset, pending enforcement actions, penalties for earlier violations, and registry duties may lapse. The general saving statute (1 U.S.C. 109) addresses repeal, and whether it covers expiration is uncertain. The sunset also runs from enactment, not the effective date, leaving roughly 9.5 years of operation.

29. **Sec. 7(a), lifting mechanism [Challenge].** The bill doesn't require NASEM to prepare the report, set a deadline, or provide funding or scope. "Serious harm" is undefined. A joint resolution needs presidential signature or a veto override, and there are no expedited procedures. This supports an argument that the stated path to lifting the prohibition is illusory.

## Effective date and structure (Sec. 8 and general)

30. **Sec. 8, 180-day delay [Loophole].** The delay gives operators a window to ramp up production, sign offtake deals, obtain licenses, and reposition vessels. There is no anti-surge or anti-evasion provision and no wind-down rule for non-grandfathered activity.

31. **Whole bill, no severability clause [Challenge].** If Sec. 2(1)(B) or 5(a) were struck down, it's uncertain whether the rest survives. The bill also has no findings, judicial review provision, rule of construction, or appropriation or authorization for NOAA.

32. **Whole bill, other undefined terms [Enforcement].** "Operator," "seabed," "mining" (Sec. 3(b)), "environmental assessment," and "serious harm" are all undefined, adding to the interpretive disputes above.

## Notes for use

- **Legal cites:** The references to DSHMRA, OCSLA, 18 U.S.C. 1001, 1 U.S.C. 109, and the Excessive Fines and takings theories are issue-spotting. Have outside counsel verify them before they go into anything external.
- **Version check:** I worked only from the text you pasted. Compare it against the official manager's amendment before relying on any section cites.
- **Strategy:** Items such as 1, 7, 10, 11, 16, and 30 are gaps sponsors could close by amendment, and raising them at markup could strengthen the bill. Items such as 4, 6, 15, 23, 27, and 31 work better as arguments that the text isn't ready, because they involve vagueness, overbreadth, and internal inconsistency.
- **Our position:** Sec. 3(b) turns on whether Meridian's licenses were issued before enactment and whether any pending applications fall outside it. That should be confirmed internally.

I can turn this into a one-page markup memo or draft amendment-opposition talking points if that would help.
